chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Khalid from al-Fudayl ibn Ghazwan said:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and al-Tayyar said to him: 'My son Hamzah found a dinar during the tawaf (circumambulation), its writing had worn off.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is his.'

28 - Ali ibn Mahziyar from Muhammad ibn Rajaa' al-Khayyat said: 'I wrote to him: I was in the Masjid al-Haram and saw a dinar, so I reached for it to take it, and behold, there was another. Then I moved the pebbles, and behold, there was a third. I took them and announced them (as lost property), but no one recognized them. What do you command me regarding that? I am your ransom.'
He said: 'He wrote to me: I have understood what you mentioned regarding the two dinars, under my mention of the place of the two dinars.'
Then he wrote under the story of the third: 'If you are in need, give the third in charity; and if you are wealthy, give all of them in charity.'
The one who seeks it (the finder) is its guarantor.

key_terms.دِينَار: A gold coin, used here as a unit of currency
key_terms.ضَامِن: Guarantor, one who is responsible for an item
key_terms.لُقَطَة: Lost property found on the ground

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on found money in Islam if the owner does not claim it?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the specific jurisprudence of *luqata* (found property) within the sacred precincts of the Kaaba, where the loss of identifying marks (*khitaba*) transfers ownership to the finder as a guarantor (*damin*). The text further distinguishes between the handling of multiple found items based on the finder's economic status: a needy individual retains one dinar while donating the rest, whereas a wealthy person is encouraged to donate all found items in charity, reflecting the Shia emphasis on social welfare and the sanctity of the Haram.
